clue.text: Something to eat? Make ultimately tasty bite

parts.note: a make is a brand, as in a make of car

indicators.note: ultimately points to the very end of the next word, its final letter

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken
to snap is to bite quickly

explanation.surface: A question about food, then a recipe tip: make sure each mouthful tastes good.
explanation.walkthrough: A brandy snap is a thin, crisp rolled ginger biscuit, often filled with cream, popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy snap is a sweet biscuit, so it is literally a thing you can eat; the question mark flags the vague definition.

parts.note: to be is to stay or exist, as in let it be

indicators.note: an empty word has lost its inside, leaving its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Have a drink but stay very quiet and hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: Bevy (or bevvy) is British slang for an alcoholic drink, short for beverage.
explanation.definitionFit: Bevy is informal British slang for a beverage, typically a beer or other alcoholic drink.

indicators.note: to cook something is to cook up or falsify it, so the letters are reworked
most of the word is used, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: the word that loses its end

explanation.surface: An instruction to cook nearly all of some exotic fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Tropical looks part of the definition, but it is the fodder; the fruit itself is not tropical.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is an orange stone fruit related to the peach and plum.

indicators.note: behaving strangely suggests oddly rearranged letters

explanation.surface: An odd pudding to find in a slimming plan.
explanation.walkthrough: Just desserts is a phrase for deserved punishment, but just is the definition here.
explanation.definitionFit: Disinterested means impartial and unbiased, which is what a just judge or ruling is.

clue.text: One might be served bean soup that's off

indicators.note: food that is off has gone bad, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

explanation.surface: A diner warned that the soup on the menu has gone bad.
explanation.walkthrough: Served suggests a waiter, but writs are served on people too.
explanation.definitionFit: A subpoena is a legal writ ordering attendance in court, and such orders are formally served on a person.

parts.note: a part is a bit or piece of something

explanation.surface: Something only slightly far away.
explanation.walkthrough: A bit reads as somewhat, but the two words split.
explanation.definitionFit: Apart means separated by a distance, so two things far apart are remote from each other.

clue.text: Something to look through belonging to Mr Goodman?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a glass piece in a camera or spectacles
second meaning: the possessive of Len, as for Len Goodman, the Strictly Come Dancing judge

explanation.surface: A puzzle about which object a certain Mr Goodman owns.
explanation.walkthrough: Len Goodman was head judge on the BBC dance show Strictly Come Dancing; the possessive Len's, without its apostrophe, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lens is the glass piece in spectacles or a camera that a person peers through to see.

clue.text: Smoothing things out late in the day

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the time between afternoon and night

explanation.walkthrough: The same spelling is a verb form of even and the noun for nightfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Levelling a surface is evening it, and the latter part of the day before night is called evening.

definitions.meaning: small, as a Scot might say, so little and dear
a British term of endearment, as in 'ta, ducks'

explanation.walkthrough: Ducks is not the bird but the affectionate form of address used in the English Midlands and North.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetheart is a fond term of address, the same use as calling someone ducks or duckie.

clue.text: First of all very ill, really unwell, sick — with this?

definitions.text: First of all very ill, really unwell, sick — with this?

indicators.note: first of all takes the opening letter of each following word in turn

parts.note: the first of five words whose opening letters are read off

explanation.surface: Someone feeling terrible asks whether this is the cause of their illness.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and a description of the answer: someone very ill might well have this.
explanation.definitionFit: A virus is a microscopic infectious agent that commonly makes people sick, so it fits the picture of illness.

clue.text: Swear as sheep and lamb going astray

indicators.note: wandering off the path, so these letters stray into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A farmer cursing because a sheep and its lamb have wandered off.
explanation.definitionFit: To blaspheme is to speak profanely, which is one sense of swearing, using oaths irreverently.

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A cricket fan annoyed that rain has held up play.
explanation.definitionFit: To procrastinate is to put off doing something, which is a form of deferring or stalling.

definitions.meaning: a performer who gives an audience a show
read not as provision but as the adverb of supple: bending in a supple way

explanation.walkthrough: Supply looks like a noun meaning provision, but here it is the adverb from supple; a performer who entertains by bending supply is a contortionist.
explanation.definitionFit: A contortionist is a circus or stage performer who amuses audiences by twisting the body into extreme, flexible shapes.

indicators.note: something failing has broken down, so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written; BT is British Telecom

explanation.surface: The telecoms company conceals why its service keeps breaking down.
explanation.walkthrough: BT is the British telephone company.
explanation.definitionFit: To obfuscate is to make something obscure or unclear, which conceals its meaning.

parts.note: bit is a past tense of bite, so having eaten into something

explanation.surface: An exclamation about someone who ate birds, and plenty of other things too.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes one kind of bird from another; the tail 'and others!' says the result is different birds again.
explanation.definitionFit: Bitterns are wading birds of the heron family known for their booming call, so they are further birds.

clue.text: Way of speaking in Oxford, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a regional accent, especially Irish
second meaning: an Oxford is a laced shoe, and a decorated one of that style is this

explanation.surface: A remark on how people talk in the university city of Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford is not the city: an Oxford is a laced shoe, and a brogue is a decorated shoe of that kind, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: A brogue is a regional accent, especially an Irish or Scottish lilt, so a manner of speech.

clue.text: On back, on back in shop?

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in business letters
a tail is the back end of something

indicators.note: back tells us to turn the second piece round so it reads the other way

parts.note: re again, meaning concerning or on the subject of

explanation.surface: A cryptic instruction about something lying on its back in a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated phrase looks like a typo, but each half does a different job.
explanation.definitionFit: A retailer sells goods to the public, so a retailer is someone found working in a shop.

indicators.note: something bad has gone wrong, so the letters of the next word are spoiled into a new order

explanation.surface: A poor outcome, perhaps an election, for a region of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulster is one of the four historic provinces of Ireland, often used for Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulster is the northern of Ireland's four traditional provinces, alongside Leinster, Munster and Connacht.

parts.note: since can mean because, as seeing that does
RE is the British school subject Religious Education

explanation.surface: A justification that what was taught in RE lessons is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the British school subject Religious Education.
explanation.definitionFit: Sincere means genuine and honest, as in true feelings or a true friend.

clue.text: The compiler, a more confident ruler?

parts.note: the setter refers to themself, so me
surer is the comparative of sure

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of being a more assured monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruler looks like a sovereign, but it is the measuring stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruler is a straight-edged strip for measuring lengths, so it is literally a measuring device.

parts.note: to run something is to conduct or manage it
a sack is a large bag

explanation.surface: A security check on someone's luggage was carried out.
explanation.definitionFit: To ransack is to search a place thoroughly and roughly, often leaving it in disorder.

clue.text: Dismay about men initially fleeing huge country

parts.note: c is short for circa, Latin for about

indicators.note: a letter that flees has left the word, so it is removed

parts.note: monster as an adjective means enormous

indicators.note: initially takes just the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: the word whose first letter goes

explanation.surface: Alarm over men escaping from some vast land.
explanation.walkthrough: The huge country reads as one phrase, monster nation, with the first letter of men dropped from monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Consternation is a feeling of anxiety or shock, closely matching dismay as a synonym.

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard over the air, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: ray (or re) is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Mentioning some points again on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray is the second note of the tonic sol-fa scale (do, re, mi), also spelt re.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise a topic or a child is to bring it up, a direct synonym in both senses.

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the next word is replaced by one that is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: Posing without clothes, apparently.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something is to tolerate it, so I can't stand it means I can't bear it.

clue.text: Drill team working machine for exercise

indicators.note: working means being put to work and reworked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A training squad running through drills on gym equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill is a gym apparatus with a moving belt that a person walks or runs on for fitness.

indicators.note: only something of these words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the words that hold the answer

explanation.surface: Witnessing a bit of an Israeli spy at work.
explanation.walkthrough: Saw looks like the past tense of see, but it is the noun for a saying; Mossad is Israel's intelligence service.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old proverb or maxim, so an adage is the same kind of traditional saying.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, cast off, as a snake does its skin
second meaning: a simple outbuilding, such as a garden hut

explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the town west of London, but it is the verb meaning cast off.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for discarding, as of skin or leaves, and a noun for a small wooden storage hut.

clue.text: RIP Yank and old Queen — it might make one cry

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, for the late Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: An American, a rest-in-peace and a former monarch: a sad story.
explanation.walkthrough: RIP looks like the epitaph and Yank like an American; both are verbs here.
explanation.definitionFit: A tearjerker is a sentimental film or story designed to bring its audience to tears.
